title: Five blessings of walking
hookLine: stamina for travel, for effort, good health, good digestion, lasting concentration
last: THE TURN — THE TURN COUNTS TOO.

cards: Some families have a tradition: after the big dinner, everyone goes for a slow walk around the block. Nobody calls it medicine. It's just what you do.
Your stomach settles, the conversation gets easier. It turns out the Buddha had his own list of reasons to walk, and one of them would make a grandmother nod.
A short discourse in the Anguttara Nikaya, the numbered collection, in the book of fives, lists five blessings of walking meditation. And they're wonderfully practical.

teach.b: It's called the Cankama Sutta, the walking discourse, AN 5.29. One: you can endure long journeys.
In the texts the Buddha and his monks travel on foot from town to town; this is stamina for that road. Two: you can endure striving.
The effort of practice, the long hours of sitting, the steady work of the path all come easier to a body used to walking. Three: you're healthy. Four: what you eat and drink is well digested.
That's the one the grandmother likes. Five: the concentration you gain while walking lasts a long time. That last one is worth slowing down for.
The discourse simply says it lasts a long time.

One way teachers explain it: concentration built while sitting perfectly still can scatter the moment you stand up, but concentration built while moving, feet lifting and placing, the body turning, is already used to movement, so it may hold up better when you get on with your day.
Notice what kind of list this is. Nothing hidden or otherworldly.
A teacher telling his students, in plain terms: this is good for your body, good for your practice, and good for the rest of your life.
The Pali texts speak about the body in more than one way; elsewhere they ask monks to reflect on its impermanence and unattractiveness. But here it isn't something to escape or despise.
It's the vehicle for the path, and walking keeps it in working order. Today's practice fits the fourth blessing exactly: a slow walk after a meal. Not for steps on a tracker.
Just to let the body settle.

how: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners who do walking meditation sometimes walk after meals, and teachers cite the five benefits from the Anguttara Nikaya's walking discourse.

o: a collected, steady mind that can stay put
a trance where you lose track of the world
a blank mind with no thoughts in it at all

games.q: the five blessings — tap the pairs.
p: food and drink are well digested

s: its five blessings are practical: stamina, health, digestion, lasting concentration.
good digestion is one of the five blessings
what you eat and drink is well digested: the fourth.
the walking discourse says concentration gained while walking lasts a long time
that's the fifth blessing; the sutta itself doesn't say more about why.

games.q: you've just finished a big meal. what does the walking discourse suggest?
o: sit very still for an hour.
games.why: among walking's five blessings is that food and drink are well digested: a slow walk after a meal fits exactly.

practice: If you can, walk slowly on your few paces of floor, a little slower than normal, feeling the whole body walking, the feet, the legs, the belly, the breath, with no labels unless you want them, as if you'd just finished a good meal and had nowhere to be.
At each turn, stand for a breath. If you're seated, feel the body breathing and the feet on the floor.

wordCard.voice: Samadhi. Concentration, collectedness: the fifth blessing of walking meditation, the kind that lasts long after you stop.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: concentration, collectedness; the fifth blessing is samadhi that lasts.

carryVoice: Your line: walking steadies. The body is the vehicle for the path. One hundred twenty days now.

sources.ref: AN 5.29, Cankama Sutta: the five benefits of walking meditation
